newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Odds shorten for Iberian EMU entry on tim.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Odds shorten for Iberian EMU entry on tim.

text.p: Forecasters have shortened the odds on Spain and Portugal winning early membership of Europe's single currency but both countries are still considered unlikely to make the grade, recent Reuters surveys have shown.
Spain and Portugal are gaining support but a majority of experts polled do not believe they will be part of Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) from the start in January 1999.

Since October, Reuters has asked economists and think-tanks in 15 European countries on a monthly basis to state which countries would form the launch pad for EMU. The latest update was published on Friday.
Almost a third of respondents believe Spain will win first-wave membership, compared with just six percent in October.
Portugal is also looking much less of a risk. In October, only eight percent of analysts reckoned it would help form a single currency. This number has now risen to 29 percent.
"They will be meeting all the Maastricht criteria so they won't be excluded. If they meet it, then they're in," said Juli Collins-Thompson, economist at Yamaichi in London.
Analysts said it was problems in northern Europe, particularly Germany, that were improving Iberia's chances.

German unemployment hit a post-war high of 4.66 million in January and the resultant spiralling dole costs have raised the possibility Europe's largest economy might fail to meet the economic criteria necessary for EMU membership.
If a compromise is reached for Germany, argue the analysts, then it cannot be denied to other European countries.
"The greater the difficulties within northern Europe, the better for southern European countries," said Brian Venables, senior bond strategist at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam.
"Portugal and Spain are so almost nearly there, that it would be very difficult to refuse them," he added.
Spain and Portugal have striven hard to meet the strict yardsticks for EMU entry. Both countries have drastically cut their budgets in an effort to instill fiscal discipline.
But despite the bullish signs, a majority in the survey still reckon Madrid and Lisbon will have a fight on their hands if they want to have their economies up to scratch for EMU membership.
Although economic fundamentals are good, they have been tarred with the same brush as Italy, viewed by the vast majority in the Reuters poll as unacceptable for monetary union in 1999.
"Portugal and Spain would perhaps be acceptable. The trouble is you cannot separate out Italy," said Klaus Baader, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
